Patient-reported symptoms:
  Triggers: Crowding: Crowded places, Spatial Triggers: Physical locations, Olfactory (Alcohol): Alcohol smell
  Maladaptive Strategies: Punishment Thinking: I tell myself I deserve to suffer because of what happened, Avoid Friends: avoid seeing friends, Avoid Circumstances: Being in circumstances that remind me of the event (eg, being in the dark).
  Memory: Bodily Reenactment: When memories come to mind of what happened, I feel my body is in the same position as when the frightening event occurred., Story Feels Unreal: The memory is so extreme it is hard to believe it actually happened to me, Visual Memories: My memories of the frightening event are mostly pictures or images.
  Negative Appraisals: Lost Happiness: I used to be a happy person but now I am always miserable., Belong Nowhere: I no longer belong anywhere, Isolation: I feel isolated and set apart from others

Vignette:
James Carter was thirty when the hurricane broke the levee. He stood on the concrete promenade of the coastal naval base, watching the water swallow the streetlights one by one. His memories arrived as sharp photographs: the way the floodwaters pressed against his chest, the silhouette of a support beam buckling overhead, the dim emergency lights casting long shadows. He felt the cold seep through his boots, his shoulders curling inward as if bracing against a wall that never stopped rising. When the evacuation order sounded, he moved with the stampede through the gymnasium doors, his back pressed to the metal railing, the thick scent of spilled whiskey from the ruptured supply warehouse clinging to his damp uniform. To James, the event felt so extreme that sometimes he questioned whether he had actually lived it. He told himself later that he deserved the weight that followed, that surviving alone in the rising dark meant he had carried a quiet debt. Over the months, the physical locations of the base became charged territories. The narrow corridor outside his officer’s quarters, the steel stairwell leading to the lower decks, the specific corner of the mess hall where the wind used to howl through the open bay doors—each one pulled him back to that day. When the gymnasium doors opened at a base reunion, the crush of bodies against his ribs made his breath catch. He could still smell the alcohol on his collar, not just from the spill that day but from every casual toast he passed. He began skipping weekend gatherings, telling his wife he had administrative work, though his desk cleared quickly. He avoided the dark, preferring the steady hum of fluorescent lights over the deepening shadows of the evening watch. During night watches, he often stood alone on the forward deck, carefully sidestepping the shadows near the bulkhead, while the rest of the crew moved through the lit corridors below. Friends’ invitations piled up, unanswered, until the silence between them felt like a natural boundary. James had come to believe he no longer belonged anywhere. The ship felt too familiar yet strangely foreign; the base a place he passed through rather than inhabited, his home a quiet room he occupied but did not truly share. He noticed that his body still remembered the exact posture of the flood—knees slightly bent, weight forward, hands ready to push—so that standing in a crowded deck or a dimly lit briefing room carried the same physical weight as that day, a quiet, unspoken reenactment. His past life felt like a photograph he could no longer step into, and he moved through his days with a quiet misery that felt as settled as his posture. Now, at thirty-four, James sits in a clinician’s office, the late afternoon light catching the edges of his uniform jacket. He has not stopped serving, but the space around him has narrowed. What frightens him most is not the dark or the crowd, but the steady conviction that his isolation is the price of what he survived. He hopes to find a way back to the people he left behind, though he is not yet sure whether he is walking toward them or simply learning to carry the distance.
